title: Designing your practice
hook: a place, a cue, a tiny start and an inner reason: the habit days, gathered into one plan

segments.voice: Yesterday: kind after a lapse. A missed day met with a gentle word instead of a scolding. Did you try that on yourself, even once? Day one thousand three hundred two.

A carpenter doesn't build a bookshelf by staring at a pile of wood and hoping. There's a sketch first. A few lines on the back of an envelope: how tall, which wall, where the screws go. The habit days have handed over a lot of wood. Habits live in places. A cue sets them off. Tiny starts beat heroic ones. A reason of your own outlasts a prize. A slip can be met kindly. This is the last day of the week, and it's a good day for the envelope. Today the pieces become one sketch, small enough to fit on a sticky note.
screen: `NO SHELF WITHOUT A SKETCH.` → `A PILE OF GOOD WOOD.` → `TODAY: ONE SKETCH.`

segments.voice: The design has four parts, and each one came from a day on this path. First, a place. The habit research kept finding that routines cling to settings: the same chair, the same corner, the same window. So the design starts with where. Not "somewhere quiet". This chair. This step on the back porch. Second, a cue. A habit needs a doorbell. The when-then days put it plainly: when this happens, then I do that. After the kettle clicks, I sit. After I park the car, I take three breaths before opening the door. The cue is something that already happens every day, so the new thing can ride on it. Third, a tiny start. Small enough that a tired, distracted, grumpy version of you could still do it. One breath. One line read. One minute. It can grow later; the job now is to make showing up nearly automatic. Fourth, an inner reason. Not a reward, not a streak, not a score. A sentence that's yours. "Because I want to be less sharp with my kids." "Because the mornings feel crowded." The research on motivation suggested that reasons from within tend to last longer than prizes from outside. Long before any lab, the Stoic teacher Epictetus put the whole idea in a line, as George Long translated it: "Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running." Design doesn't do the walking. It just makes the first step easy to find.
screen: `A PLACE: THIS CHAIR, THIS CORNER.` · `A CUE: WHEN THIS, THEN THAT.` · then, large: `A TINY START.` · then: `A REASON OF YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your design. If you have a pen or a phone, keep it close. Settle for a few breaths first. Then fill in four short blanks, in your head or on paper. Where: the exact spot. When: the cue that comes right before. What: the tiny start, so small it's almost silly. Why: one honest sentence. Read the four lines back once. Then let them rest, and sit with the breath for the time that's left. The bell holds the time.
Designing your practice. Four lines: a place, a cue, a tiny start and a reason of your own, so the practice has somewhere to live. Today's word.
Your line: my design. Today, put your four lines somewhere you'll see them tomorrow morning, and change one word if it doesn't fit your real life. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: People building a regular practice often write a short plan naming the place, the cue that comes before it, a very small first step and their own reason, and keep it where they'll see it; Stoic teachers like Epictetus treated character as built by repeated action.
